title: Formulas as Characters
tagline: A clerk in a patent office changed physics in one year. You will turn five famous formulas into short scenes you can read like a sentence.
card: How to keep a formula by understanding it first, then giving each symbol a character and each operation an action.
goal: you will turn five formulas into stories where each symbol is a character, read the formulas back from the stories, and learn why meaning comes first.

left_off.q: What is the first letter of the code word for T? And for Q?
How many pegs does the alphabet system have?
How would you use the pegs for a procedure with six steps?
left_off.a: Put each step on a peg A to F, as an action on the peg.

story.heading: The clerk who changed the world in a year

text: Bern, Switzerland, 1905. A young man in his twenties sits at a high desk in the patent office, reading other people's ideas for new machines. He is a clerk, and nobody thinks of him as a scientist. At home, in his spare time, he is thinking about the nature of light, time and space.

In that one year he sent four papers to a leading German journal. Any one of them would have made his name. They explained how light carries energy in small packets, how tiny particles in water jiggle, how time and space change at high speed, and, in a short paper at the end of the year, how mass and energy are connected. His name was Albert Einstein.

check.a: He was a clerk in a patent office in Bern, working on physics in his spare time.

parts.talk: What would you do with spare time and a hard question? Would you work on it alone, or with other people?

text: The last paper gave the world the most famous formula ever written: E = mc². Energy equals mass times the speed of light, squared. Five characters, and yet they say that a tiny amount of matter holds an enormous amount of energy.

Millions of people know this formula without knowing what it means. And that is a clue to something about memory. You can remember a formula as a picture of symbols, but if you do not understand it, it will not last, and you will not know when to use it. A formula is a sentence. First understand what it says.

check.a: Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared: a little mass holds a huge amount of energy.

parts.talk: Explain E = mc² in your own words, as if to a ten-year-old.

text: Once you understand a formula, the problem is the symbols. E, m, c, a little 2: they look like nothing. They are abstract, and we found in the last rooms what the mind does with abstract things: it lets go.
So we give them life. Each symbol becomes a character, each operation an action, and the whole formula becomes a short scene. It sounds silly, and it is: that is what makes it work.

check.a: Symbols are abstract, and abstract things are forgotten. A character you can picture holds them.

parts.talk: Which formulas or rules do you still remember from school? How do you remember them?

words.m: a rule written in symbols. A formula for the area of a circle.
a sign that stands for something else. E is the symbol for energy.
to multiply a number by itself. Four squared is sixteen.
the amount of matter in an object.
the distance from the centre of a circle to its edge.
the distance round the outside of a circle.

source: Einstein's 1905 papers: the mass-energy paper appeared in the same year as the other three. Told here in our own words.

method.x: Understand the formula first. Then make it a scene.

items.x: In words, in one sentence. 'Force equals mass times acceleration.'
Use the first letter or the meaning: E = eagle (energy), m = mouse (mass).
'=' is a balance or a table; '×' is a crossing; '²' is a twin or a square box; '+' is a joining.
The characters, in the same order as the formula, doing the actions.
Put in simple numbers and check the result. If it works, the formula is yours.

head: Formula
Meaning
The scene
rows: Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared
An Eagle is carried by a Mouse riding a Cheetah, twice round the track.
A Fist hits a Mouse and he flies away like an Arrow.
In a right-angled triangle, the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the square on the longest side
A ladder (c) leans against a wall (a) and a floor (b): two small gardens plus a medium one fill one big garden.
Circumference equals two times pi times the radius
A Cheetah runs twice round a giant Pie (π) with a Rabbit in the middle.
Area equals pi times the radius squared
A pie cut into a perfect circle: a Rabbit, twice, sits on top of the pie (π): that is the Area.

method.title: E = mc² as a scene
lines: A balance, or a table where it sits.
A cheetah (the speed of light, the fastest thing there is).
Twice round: two laps, or two cheetahs.
method.pic: An eagle is perched on a balance, and a tiny mouse riding a cheetah races round twice, lifting the eagle sky-high.

items: Understand first. A picture of a formula you do not understand will fade; a picture of one you do will stay.
Check with numbers. If the sides of a triangle are 3 and 4, the longest side is 5: 9 + 16 = 25.
Say it in words. If you can say it, you can build the scene.
Review formulas the way you review any list: soon, then at longer gaps.

method.x: Say each of the five formulas aloud in words, then tell the scene for one of them.

try.title: Symbols and characters
try.prompt: Match each symbol to the character used in the scenes above.

items.s: F = ma means force equals ___ times acceleration.
In a right-angled triangle with shorter sides 3 and 4, the longest side is ___.
The circumference of a circle is 2 × pi × the ___.

try.title: Build F = ma
try.prompt: Write your own scene for F = ma. Use a character for each symbol, and an action for each operation.
try.model: A giant Fist is punching a Mouse across the room. The mouse flies away faster and faster like an Arrow. The harder the fist (force), the faster the mouse goes.
checks: There is a character for F, m and a.

try.title: Build the Pythagorean theorem
try.prompt: Make one scene for a² + b² = c². Then test it with 3, 4 and 5.
try.model: A ladder (c) leans on a wall (a) with its foot on the floor (b). The wall's garden (a-squared) and the floor's garden (b-squared) are poured into the ladder's giant square (c-squared), and exactly fill it. Test: 9 + 16 = 25.
checks: The plus and equals are actions.

try.title: Two circle formulas
try.prompt: Make scenes for C = 2πr and A = πr². Make sure the two scenes are different enough not to mix.
try.model: C: a Cheetah runs twice round a giant Pie with a Rabbit in the middle. A: a Rabbit sits on a pie, twice, and that is the Area of the pie. Give C a race and A a picnic.
checks: The two scenes are clearly different.
Each has characters for each symbol.
I can say which formula each is.

try.q: A formula you do not understand but have memorised as a picture will...
opts: Be easy to use for years
Probably fade, and be hard to apply
try.why: Meaning is what keeps a formula and tells you when to use it.

try.title: Teach it
try.prompt: Explain one of the five formulas to an imaginary student in one minute: what it says, the scene, and a number example.
